draft.title: Contour lines
card: A topographic map shows the shape of the land. A contour line is a line that joins places of the same height above sea level.
Every point on one contour line is at the same height. Numbers written on the lines give that height in metres.
Where contour lines are close together, the land is steep because the height changes over a short distance.
Where contour lines are far apart, the land is gentle because the height changes slowly over a long distance.
draft.remember: Close lines mean a steep slope. Wide gaps mean a gentle slope.

a.q: A student traces one contour line on a topographic map. What is true of every point along that line?
opts: They are all at the same height above sea level
They are all the same distance from the coast
They all have the same steepness of slope
They all have the same type of vegetation
a.why: A contour line joins points of equal height above sea level. Steepness is shown by how close the lines are to each other, not by what one line joins.
a.clue: Think about what the number on the line tells you.

b.q: Sam studies a map of Mount Kosciuszko in the Snowy Mountains, NSW. The contour lines are very close together on the eastern side and far apart on the western side. What does this show?
opts: The east side is steep and the west side is gentle
The east side is gentle and the west side is steep
The east side is higher than the west side
The east side is flat and the west side is a cliff
b.why: Lines close together show that height changes quickly, so the land is steep. Lines far apart show a gentle slope. The spacing shows steepness, not which side is higher.
b.clue: Close lines mean the height changes over a short distance.

a.best: They are all at the same height above sea level

b.best: The east side is steep and the west side is gentle

problems.detail: The question uses a real place, Mount Kosciuszko, but reverses its real terrain. The western side of the Main Range (the Western Fall into the Geehi valley) is the steep side, and the eastern side slopes more gently. As written, the question would teach students a false fact about Kosciuszko. Use a made-up hill, or swap the sides.
